newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian industry welcomes 25 pct white sugar duty.
newsitem.headline: Russian industry welcomes 25 pct white sugar duty.

text.p: Russia's decision to slap a 25 percent duty on most refined sugar imports from May 15 should go a long way towards shoring up ailing Russian refineries, traders and industry representatives said on Wednesday.
But alone it would not provide a miracle cure for the sugar sector, which has been buffeted in recent years by cheap imports from neighbouring Ukraine, they said.
"To protect the domestic sugar industry, this decree was a very important and very necessary step," Vasily Severin, head of the Rossakhsvyokla sugar producers' association said.
The decree, released to the press on Tuesday, applies to white sugar from all destinations except Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgystan, which have a customs treaty with Russia.

Severin said that the duty will replace a plan put forward by the Foreign Trade Ministry last year calling for quotas on Russian white sugar imports to the tune of 1.5 million tonnes overall, of which 1.15 million would come from Ukraine.
"There will be no quotas this year -- we do not need them, now that we have the duty," he said. "But this step alone should be enough to protect our industry," he added.
Some traders were less hopeful, arguing that while the duty was a boon for Russian refineries, problems would not simply disappear after May 15, when it comes into force.
"The key change in this decree is that it includes Ukraine," said one Moscow-based sugar trader. "It is a measure that will help, but it won't be enough in itself."
Trading companies holding sugar could also benefit from the move, a second dealer said.
"One result of this duty is that sugar prices within Russia will rise as supplies from Ukraine are reduced."
The second dealer said Ukrainian sugar would continue to be smuggled through Belarus to avoid higher duties, limiting the impact of the government decree.
But he did not think sugar stocks in Ukraine were high enough to trigger a surge in smuggled exports to Russia.
"Stocks in Ukraine are low enough to suggest that there will not be that much coming in (through Belarus)," he said. "Closer integration between Belarus and Russia will also help cut down smuggling."
Russia and Belarus signed a watered-down Union Treaty earlier this month.
The Russian sugar industry has been lobbying the government hard for protectionist measures it says it needs to survive in the face of cheap competition, particularly from Ukraine.
Severin said he and other sugar industry representatives had written a joint letter to President Boris Yeltsin and the government, describing the crisis facing the sector.
The letter said that without government support, the Russian sugar industry faced "total collapse."
He said the letter may have speeded up the government's protectionist step of introducing the duty.

Last year Russia imported 1.70 million tonnes of raws and 1.44 million tonnes of whites, the bulk of which came from Ukraine. It also produces around 2.0 million tonnes a year from its own beet production.
Official data show January-February imports of raw and white sugar in 1997 are running well behind year-ago levels.
Traders said raw imports were down partly because of delays in oil-for-sugar barter deals between Russia and Cuba.
White sugar imports early last year were high, and in 1997 traders were less keen to take delivery, they added.
"Last year there were a lot of white sugar imports early on, and people just lost money," said a dealer.
